lead: Polymorphism lets one operation name work on different types. In Python the object's class chooses the method at runtime, so a single call like shape.area() runs the right code for a circle or a rectangle. Operator overloading applies the same idea to symbols: writing m1 + m2 can call your own __add__ method. Duck typing goes further and asks only for a method name, not a class. These ideas make Python code short and flexible, and they appear in libraries, calculators, money and unit classes, and menu-driven programs.
prereq: You need: 4.1 to 4.5, plus lambda, map, filter and reduce from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Polymorphism means one operation name can be used with objects of different classes. The caller writes shape.area() and does not test the class. Python looks at the object's class and runs that class's area() method. The method body is chosen when the call runs, not when the code is written. This is dynamic dispatch. 4.5 shows the lookup order.

Built-in functions are already polymorphic. len('abc') is 3, len([1, 2, 3]) is 3, and len({'a': 1}) is 1. Each type supplies its own __len__. A user function total_area(shapes) can loop and call shape.area() on each item; it works for Circle, Rectangle, or any object with an area() method. A subclass that overrides a parent method changes the behaviour for its own objects while the call site stays the same. Some syllabi call this dynamic polymorphism.

Operator overloading gives an operator such as + or < a meaning for your class. Python translates the symbol into a call to a special method with two leading and two trailing underscores. Writing m1 + m2 calls m1.__add__(m2) and uses the returned object. The original objects are not changed; __add__ should build and return a new object. __sub__ and __mul__ work the same way. __eq__ defines ==, __lt__ defines <, __str__ defines what print() shows, and __len__ defines len(). Defining __eq__ also lets lists of your objects compare correctly. Python does not change the operator for other classes; only objects of your class use your method.

In the worked example, Money.__add__ adds total paise and returns a new Money. Money.__eq__ compares total paise, so 10 rupees 50 paise equals another 10 rupees 50 paise. Money.__str__ formats the value as ₹15.75. Without __eq__, == would compare identity (memory address), not value.

sections.h3: Duck typing and functions as first-class objects

blocks.text: Duck typing means Python cares about the methods an object has, not its class name. If a function calls obj.quack(), any object with a quack() method works, even if it does not inherit from a Duck class. A missing method is not caught when the function is defined. It fails only when the call runs, with AttributeError. This is why polymorphism in Python does not require a common base class.

Functions are first-class objects. You can store them in a dict, pass them as arguments, and return them. A lambda is a small unnamed function: square = lambda x: x * x. Unit 2 covers map, filter and reduce. Here note that methods are attributes, so bound methods can also be stored. A jump table maps keys to callables: ops = {'+': add, '-': sub}; ops[choice](a, b). This replaces a long if-elif chain and is common in calculators, menu programs and interpreters.

figure.caption: Two Money objects pass through __add__, which returns a new Money object with the normalised total.

spec.title: Money addition
spec.aria: Two Money objects, 10 rupees 50 paise and 5 rupees 25 paise, go through the __add__ method and produce a new Money object of 15 rupees 75 paise.

examples.question: Define a class Money with attributes rupees and paise. Normalise paise so that paise is always less than 100. Overload + to return a new Money, == to compare total paise, and str() to print ₹R.PP. Take m1 = Money(10, 50), m2 = Money(5, 25), m3 = Money(10, 50). Show the output of print(m1 + m2), print(m1 == m3) and print(m1 == m2).
steps: m1 + m2 calls __add__. Total = 1050 + 525 = 1575 paise. 1575 ÷ 100 gives 15 rupees and 1575 % 100 gives 75 paise, so the new object is Money(15, 75).
print(m1 + m2) calls __str__ on Money(15, 75) and prints ₹15.75.
m3: rupees = 10, paise = 50, total = 1050 paise. m1 == m3 calls __eq__: 1050 == 1050, so the result is True.
m1 == m2 calls __eq__: 1050 == 525, so the result is False.
examples.answer: m1 + m2 prints ₹15.75, m1 == m3 is True, and m1 == m2 is False; the sum is 1575 paise.
examples.check:
m1 = 10 * 100 + 50
m2 = 5 * 100 + 25
total = m1 + m2
print(total)
print(m1)
print(m2)

traps: Thinking polymorphism needs a common base class. Duck typing works from method names alone; a missing method is caught only when it is called.
Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes objects unhashable in a set or as a dict key. Define __hash__ if you need hashing.
Returning None from __add__ or changing self instead of returning a new object. a + b should produce a value; print(a + b) would show None otherwise.
Confusing __str__ with __repr__. __str__ is for users and print(); __repr__ is for developers and the interactive prompt.
Writing m1 + 5 when __add__ expects a Money object. total_paise() then fails with AttributeError unless you handle other types or return NotImplemented.

quiz.q: Which special method does Python call for the expression a + b?
quiz.a: Python tries a.__add__(b). If that fails, it may try b.__radd__(a) for some operands.

quiz.q: Why can len() work on strings, lists and your own class?
quiz.a: Each type provides a __len__ method. len() calls that method at runtime, so the same name has different bodies for different classes.

quiz.q: For the Money class in the worked example, what does Money(2, 130) store after normalisation?
quiz.a: 130 // 100 = 1 rupee is added to 2, and 130 % 100 = 30 paise remain. The object stores rupees = 3, paise = 30, total = 330 paise.

quiz.q: A function greet(obj) calls obj.speak(). It is called with a Robot class that has no speak(). When does the error appear and what is it?
quiz.a: The error appears at the call obj.speak(), not when greet is defined. Python raises AttributeError: 'Robot' object has no attribute 'speak'.

quiz.q: What is a jump table and why use it instead of a long if-elif chain?
quiz.a: A jump table is a dict mapping keys to functions, such as ops[key](args). It avoids long if-elif chains and is easy to extend with a new key-function pair.

quiz.q: Given f = lambda x: x * 2 and nums = [1, 2, 3], what does list(map(f, nums)) produce?
quiz.a: map applies f to each item. The results are 2, 4 and 6, so the list is [2, 4, 6].

beyond: Not for the exam. Operator overloading is how libraries such as NumPy make + work on whole arrays and how pandas adds columns. Duck typing underpins Python's protocol-based design: file-like objects, iterables and context managers are recognised by methods, not by base classes. Python's data model, built on these dunder methods, is the foundation of those protocols. Search for 'Python data model', 'protocol-oriented programming' and 'functools.singledispatch' to go further.
